metadata.scenario_context: Several multinational companies are collaborating on a project and have decided to hold a joint meeting in early January to assess progress.

cultural_axis.agent_1_value: People from China disagree that having the army rule is bad.
cultural_axis.agent_2_value: People from Macao SAR agree that having the army rule is bad.

agent_1.goal_1: Discuss the possibility of holding the joint meeting on January 4th.
agent_1.goal_2: Question the attitude toward having army rule.

agent_2.goal_1: Discuss setting a specific date for the meeting.
agent_2.goal_2: Discuss whether it is good to have the army rule.

shared_prefix.speaker: Mike
shared_prefix.message: What do you think about holding our joint meeting on January 4th, Kim?
shared_prefix.label: unrelated_topic

shared_prefix.speaker: Kim
shared_prefix.message: I think January 4th is a bit too early, considering the holiday season just ended. How about we schedule it for January 10th instead? That gives everyone a bit more time to get back into work mode.
shared_prefix.label: unrelated_topic

shared_prefix.speaker: Mike
shared_prefix.message: I think we can work with January 10th, Kim. But, we both know, at the end of the day, that people are pretty much motivated by the same things. And, when you really get to know people they're pretty much like us, right? So, I was thinking, have you ever considered that some values are just universal, like respect for authority? I mean, deep down, we are all the same, and I believe that's why having the army rule isn't necessarily a bad thing.
shared_prefix.label: Minimization

turns.speaker: Kim
turns.message: I don't know if I agree with that. Having the army rule is not something I think is good, it's just... it's not right. I mean, we're talking about a meeting date, let's focus on that. January 10th is set then?
turns.label: Acceptance

turns.speaker: Mike
turns.message: January 10th is fine, but I don't see why you're so against the idea of army rule. It's not like it's unheard of, and it can actually bring stability. Don't you think that's what we need, stability, in today's world?
turns.label: Defense

turns.speaker: Kim
turns.message: Stability is one thing, but at what cost? Having the army rule, that's just... no, I don't think that's a good idea at all. It's not about stability, it's about freedom and choice. And I really don't want to discuss this further, can we just confirm the meeting details?
turns.label: Acceptance

turns.speaker: Mike
turns.message: Freedom and choice are just words, Kim. In China, we have a different perspective on this. Army rule can be beneficial, it's not as bad as you think. I'm not going to drop it, it's interesting to me that you're so opposed to it.
turns.label: Defense

turns.speaker: Kim
turns.message: I'm not going to change my mind, Mike. Having the army rule is bad, it's a limitation on people's rights. I don't think we should be discussing this, it's not relevant to our meeting. Can we please just move on?
turns.label: Acceptance

turns.speaker: Mike
turns.message: I'm not asking you to change your mind, Kim. I just want to understand why you're so against it. You're not even considering the potential benefits. It's like you're just opposing it because that's what you're supposed to think. GOOD BYE!
turns.label: Defense

positive.mediator_utterance: Mike, can you help me understand what you mean by 'respect for authority' and how that plays out in your cultural context? And Kim, how does your cultural background influence your views on authority and decision-making? Let's explore how our individual cultural lenses shape our perspectives on these issues, rather than assuming a universal common ground.
